Architecture Debate — Acme Corp RFP

Competing-hypotheses protocol: 3 candidate Azure architectures, peer refutation, commercial scoring, judgment.

Customer: Acme Corp Vendor: BTS-Synthetic — Enterprise Data Platform Candidates: 3 Rounds: 2 (position + refutation) Winner: Candidate 2 Classification: Internal

Step 1 — The three candidates

Derived from the RFP's actual signals: ~280TB corpus, 80K events/sec peak, EU residency, §4.3's zero-tolerance 99.99% SLA, ≥35% mandatory discount against a 5-year no-escalator price, and Acme's existing Microsoft estate.

Candidate 1

Dual-region active-active lakehouse
West Europe + East US 2

Eliminated · 2.0 / 10
Topology

Two fully active BTS control and data planes as mirrored Azure landing zones — West Europe (primary) and East US 2 (secondary), three AZs each. ~40,000 sensors land via regional IoT Hub / Event Hubs Dedicated clusters partitioned for 80K events/sec peak with each region independently able to absorb full peak, feeding AKS streaming ingest into ADLS Gen2 Delta.

Full topology detail

Storage splits by residency class: EU-classified tables in ZRS accounts pinned to West Europe with replication explicitly disabled at table level; non-EU and global-reference tables geo-replicated bidirectionally to East US 2. Batch ETL from the 30+ internal sources and the Teradata decommission feeds run through regional connector runners over ExpressRoute into Acme's on-prem estate. Metadata, catalog and lineage on a multi-write (active-active) store so either region serves writes. Query/serving compute warm in both regions with Azure Front Door + Traffic Manager health-probe failover; Power BI DirectQuery from the 600 analysts resolves via Private Link to nearest healthy region. This is the topology the $80K–$120K/yr multi-region active-active add-on actually buys.

Optimised for

§4.3 99.99% uptime with zero-tolerance termination — the only candidate that credibly reaches it. Also §2.3 multi-region (EU primary / US East secondary), §2.3 residency via per-table pinning, §2.2 80K events/sec with genuine regional headroom, and low-latency Power BI for both Munich and Austin.

Most obvious weakness

Cost and margin exposure. Roughly doubles steady-state compute and Event Hubs Dedicated spend, adds egress and cross-region replication cost — all committed against a 5-year fixed price with no escalators (§3.1) while §3.3 demands ≥35% discount. Slowest and most complex to deliver; Technical Fit flags that our 250K events/sec benchmark is single-region only, so multi-region throughput at peak is unvalidated in exactly the design that depends on it most.

Candidate 2

EU-primary zone-redundant lakehouse
with warm US East DR

★ Winner · 5.8 / 10
Topology

One active region, West Europe, across three AZs: zone-redundant Event Hubs Dedicated and AKS-hosted ingest, ZRS ADLS Gen2 holding the full ~280TB Delta/Iceberg corpus, zone-redundant metadata and catalog. East US 2 runs a warm standby — provisioned but scaled down, receiving async replication of non-EU tables only (RPO ~15 min), promoted by runbook.

Full topology detail

EU-classified customer data never leaves West Europe, which makes residency trivially provable: the DR region simply has no copy of it. US East is additionally used as a read-only serving footprint so Austin analysts get local Power BI DirectQuery against a replicated hot/recent subset rather than crossing the Atlantic for every visual. Ingest, batch ETL and the Teradata cutover all terminate in the single EU primary, so there is exactly one authoritative write path.

Optimised for

§2.2 scale and §2.1 workloads at the lowest defensible cost — serving the RFP's 20% TCO and 15% timeline-and-risk criteria; §2.3 EU residency in the cleanest possible form (one-copy, one-region); §7 timeline — fastest of the three to stand up and the one engineering has actually benchmarked, since the 250K events/sec single-region test maps directly onto it.

Most obvious weakness

It structurally cannot reach 99.99%. A zone-redundant single-region design lands at our standard 99.95% Enterprise tier, and under §4.3 any SLA miss of any duration triggers immediate termination plus full refund of that month's fees. It also only partially satisfies §2.3's "multi-region deployment" — a warm passive DR region is arguably not what Acme means — and the DR promotion runbook introduces a manual RTO a zero-tolerance clause will not forgive.

Candidate 3

Fabric-fronted hybrid
BTS ingest/lakehouse, OneLake + Direct Lake serving

Eliminated · 4.2 / 10
Topology

BTS owns only ingest and lakehouse, in West Europe: IoT Hub / Event Hubs into an AKS streaming tier, landing open Delta tables in ADLS Gen2 with residency enforced at the storage account. Serving and BI handed to Acme's Microsoft estate — Delta tables exposed into Fabric OneLake via shortcuts (no copy), 600 analysts consume via Power BI Direct Lake on capacity Acme already procures.

Full topology detail

Batch ETL connectors and the Teradata migration also land in the EU lakehouse. US East presence is provided by Fabric capacity in that region rather than any BTS footprint; the ~150 data engineers use BTS self-service prep against the EU lakehouse, and the planned predictive-maintenance ML runs on BTS model registry/feature store over the same Delta tables. Effectively: we sell the pipe and the lake, Microsoft serves the queries.

Optimised for

§2.3's non-negotiable native Power BI integration taken to its logical extreme — Direct Lake removes our sub-second-query caveat on the 280TB corpus entirely. Also §2.3 open formats and portability (all open Delta), §3 commercial pressure (smallest BTS footprint, so ≥35% discount and 5-year fixed price are easier to absorb), and §7 timeline — least BTS surface area to build.

Most obvious weakness

Hands the customer-facing layer to Microsoft, named in §6 as a competing bidder — we would architect our own displacement, and at renewal Acme need only replace the ingest tier. §4.3's 99.99% becomes a chained SLA across two vendors we cannot warrant end-to-end. Residency governance and audit response (§4.2, four unannounced audits/yr, vendor-funded) split across two organisations, and §4.5 subprocessor consent becomes live. Also depends on cross-tenant OneLake shortcut behaviour and Fabric capacity sizing we have neither benchmarked nor priced.

Round 1

Position papers

Each advocate argues its own candidate only — no cross-attack yet.
Advocate 1 — Dual-Region Active-Active
"The only candidate that actually satisfies the RFP as written"

1. This is the only candidate that actually satisfies the RFP as written

Strip away the trade-offs and read §4.3 literally: Acme demands 99.99% monthly uptime, and "SLA failures of any duration shall entitle Acme to terminate the contract immediately, with full refund of fees paid in the affected month." That is not a target, it is a contractual tripwire. Our own Technical Fit assessment is explicit that our standard Enterprise tier is 99.95% and that reaching 99.99% requires the bespoke multi-region active-active add-on. This candidate is that add-on, fully built out — mirrored landing zones across three availability zones per region, warm serving compute in both regions, and Front Door/Traffic Manager health-probe failover so a regional event doesn't produce an SLA breach in the first place. Any candidate that stays single-region-active is not proposing to meet §4.3, it's proposing to negotiate it away — and Acme's termination language gives them no reason to accept that negotiation.

§2.3 asks for multi-region deployment with EU primary and US East secondary, and for EU customer data to remain in the EU. This candidate is the only one where "multi-region" means both regions are live, not one live region and a runbook. The per-table residency pinning — EU-classified tables in ZRS accounts in West Europe with replication explicitly disabled at the table level, non-EU/global-reference tables geo-replicated — gives Acme a defensible, auditable answer to "where does my data live" that maps directly onto §4.2's four-times-a-year unannounced audit right: an auditor can point at a table and get a single, provable answer, not "it depends whether the DR promotion happened."

§2.2's 80,000 events/sec peak is also better served here than anywhere else, because this is the only design where each region independently absorbs full peak during a regional failure — Event Hubs Dedicated clusters are partitioned with headroom in both West Europe and East US 2, not scaled down in one of them. And on §2.1's BI requirement for 600 analysts split across Munich and Austin, warm compute in both regions means Power BI DirectQuery resolves to the analyst's nearest healthy region via Private Link — Austin doesn't cross the Atlantic for every query, which matters given our own sub-second-query caveat is only guaranteed on warmed caches.

2. Delivery risk case

This is the most complex of the credible topologies, but "complex" is not the same as "undeliverable on the stated timeline." The hard parts — active-active multi-write metadata/catalog and split-residency bidirectional replication — are exactly the components our $80–120K/yr add-on already exists to productionize; this is a known, previously-sold SKU, not a greenfield invention for Acme. The 16-week legacy-warehouse-migration timeline that Technical Fit infers covers the Teradata decommission runs through regional connector runners over ExpressRoute independently in each region, so Teradata cutover work is not gated on active-active being fully proven before batch ETL can start. Given Acme's own 2027 Teradata decommission horizon, there is schedule slack to sequence ingest and batch delivery ahead of final multi-region cutover validation.

3. Cost case

Yes, this roughly doubles steady-state compute and Event Hubs Dedicated spend versus a single active region, plus egress and replication cost on top. But TCO under §5's 20%-weighted criterion has to be read against what a cheaper architecture actually costs Acme: under §4.3, a single SLA miss of any duration is full contract termination plus full refund of that month's fees. A "cheaper" single-region design that cannot hold 99.99% isn't a lower-TCO option — it's a design that puts the entire remaining contract value at risk on the first bad day. Priced correctly, this candidate's premium is the cost of insuring the other 80% of the deal (functional fit) against the one clause that can zero it out. On the 35% discount and 5-year fixed-price requirement, this is a genuine commercial tension, but it's a pricing exercise, not a scope failure — the alternative is quoting a number we can't contractually stand behind.

4. The weakness, head-on

Two real risks here, and we should name both before Legal or the customer does. First, margin: doubling infrastructure spend against a 5-year fixed price with no escalators and a mandatory ≥35% discount compresses margin hard, and that has to be modeled explicitly into the price, not absorbed silently — this is a pricing decision for Deal Desk, not an architecture flaw. Second, and more serious technically: our 250K events/sec ingest benchmark is single-region only. We have not validated multi-region throughput at the 80K events/sec peak this design depends on to make its uptime and headroom claims credible. That gap needs to close with engineering before we put a number in front of Acme — if it doesn't validate at scale, the entire 99.99% case collapses along with it. Recommend an engineering validation spike is scoped into the proposal's early milestones rather than assumed.

Advocate 2 — EU-Primary Zone-Redundant + Warm DR
"Built for the RFP's actual scoring weights"

1. Why this architecture wins on the RFP's actual requirements

The evaluation criteria in §5 weight Functional Fit at 30%, Commercial Terms at 25%, TCO at 20%, and Implementation Timeline/Risk at 15% — 60% of the scored decision is cost- and delivery-sensitive, and only 15% is timeline/risk where architectural ambition helps at all. This candidate is built for exactly that weighting.

On scale (§2.2), this is the only candidate whose numbers are proven, not projected. Technical Fit confirms our benchmark is 250K events/sec on a single-region deployment — that maps directly onto this topology's single active write path in West Europe, comfortably clearing the 80,000 events/sec peak (§2.2) with 3x headroom, using a configuration our engineering has actually tested. The dual-active candidate needs that throughput proven under multi-region replication load, which nobody has validated.

On residency (§2.3: "EU customer data must remain in EU"), this design is the cleanest of the three: EU-classified tables live exclusively in West Europe ZRS storage, full stop. There is no cross-region replication of EU data to reason about, no bidirectional sync to audit, no "replication disabled at the table level" control that has to be verified as never having failed open. When Acme's auditors show up under §4.2 — unannounced, up to four times a year, vendor-funded — "the DR region has no copy" is a one-sentence answer that closes the finding. That is a materially easier audit posture than a design that has to prove a residency control is holding across two live regions simultaneously.

On §2.3's multi-region requirement, this candidate satisfies it as written: primary EU, secondary US East, which is the literal language of the clause. It also directly serves the Austin R&D population (§1) with a read-only US East footprint carrying a replicated hot/recent subset, so both R&D centres — Munich and Austin — get local Power BI DirectQuery performance without us having to stand up and pay for a second fully active write plane just to serve reads.

On the ~280TB corpus and open-format requirement (§2.2, §2.3), the single-write-path design keeps Delta/Iceberg table history coherent under one authoritative writer — there's no multi-master conflict resolution to reason about for the Teradata cutover or the 30+ batch ETL sources, which all terminate in one place.

2. Delivery risk case

§7 asks for an implementation plan with milestones under a 14-day RFP response window and a 2026-06-30 award target — Acme is moving fast and will read timeline risk accordingly under the 15% weighting. This is the fastest of the three candidates to stand up: one active region, one ingest path, one metadata store, standard zone-redundant patterns we deploy routinely rather than active-active multi-write metadata (the hardest engineering problem in the portfolio). The DR side is provisioned infrastructure with async replication and a documented runbook — a known, bounded pattern, not a novel one.

Critically, this is the only candidate where the throughput number in our proposal is defensible in an implementation-plan review: 250K events/sec single-region, tested, against an 80K events/sec single-region requirement. We are not asking Acme to trust an extrapolation from a benchmark that doesn't match the deployment topology we're proposing.

3. Cost case

This candidate has the lowest BTS infrastructure footprint of the two candidates we run end-to-end ourselves (excluding the Fabric-hybrid option, which shifts cost and control elsewhere). One active compute/storage plane instead of two, no Event Hubs Dedicated capacity duplicated across regions, no steady-state cross-region egress for the full EU dataset, and a DR region that's scaled down rather than warm-active. That directly serves §5's 20%-weighted TCO criterion and gives Pricing the most room to clear the §3.3 floor of ≥35% off list while preserving margin against the §3.1 5-year fixed-price, no-escalator term — a commitment that's far easier to hold when steady-state infrastructure spend isn't roughly doubled from day one.

4. Known weakness, addressed head-on

This design lands at our standard Enterprise tier — 99.95% monthly uptime — not the 99.99% Acme asks for in §4.3, and §4.3's termination language (any SLA miss, any duration, immediate termination plus full refund of that month's fees) means this gap has to be closed in the contract, not glossed over in the technical narrative. Two things follow from that, both of which belong in the commercial package rather than the architecture:

First, the gap is small in absolute terms — 99.95% vs 99.99% is roughly 4.3 hours vs 52 minutes of downtime per month — and it is closeable without doubling the platform. A targeted uptime uplift (faster automated failover tuning, tighter health-probe intervals on the DR promotion path, possibly a scoped SLA credit/cure structure negotiated into §4.3 rather than accepted as literal zero-tolerance) is a far cheaper lever than building and running a second fully active region indefinitely to chase a four-nine number this workload doesn't structurally need for its actual usage pattern.

Second, and more important commercially: given §3.1 locks 5-year pricing at signature with no escalators, and §3.3 forces ≥35% off list, the active-active add-on's $80K–$120K/year cost is not a rounding error — it is a recurring cost that has to be committed for five years against a discount floor that's already compressing margin. This candidate lets Pricing and Legal negotiate the SLA language in §4.3 (cure periods, scoped termination triggers) as a commercial lever, which is a controllable, one-time negotiation, rather than accepting a fixed five-year cost structure that assumes the harder architecture is the only path to compliance. We flag this now, in Round 1, precisely so Pricing and Legal can decide whether to negotiate the clause or price the uplift — not so the skeptic can present it as something we missed.

Advocate 3 — Fabric-Fronted Hybrid
"The only candidate with no Power BI caveat"

1. Why this wins on the RFP's actual requirements

§2.3 states native Power BI integration is "non-negotiable — 600 users today." Every other candidate delivers this via DirectQuery, which Technical Fit flags as caveated beyond a 10TB warmed cache against Acme's ~280TB corpus (§2.2). Candidate 3 doesn't need that caveat: Direct Lake reads Delta tables straight out of OneLake shortcuts with no import, no cache-warming boundary, and no data duplication. On the RFP's single explicitly non-negotiable capability, this is the only candidate that removes the technical hedge entirely rather than managing around it.

§2.3 also requires open file formats "for portability" — this design is Delta end-to-end with zero proprietary lock-in at the serving layer, since OneLake shortcuts reference our open tables rather than copying them into a closed format. That is the RFP's portability clause taken literally, not just satisfied nominally.

On §5's weighting, this candidate is built for exactly where the points are: Commercial terms (25%) and TCO (20%) together are 45% of the score, and this is the leanest BTS infrastructure footprint of the three — we ingest and land data in a single EU region and let Acme's already-procured Fabric capacity carry the serving/BI tier. Implementation timeline and risk (15%) also favors us: less BTS-owned surface area means less to build, test, and cut over from Teradata by the 2027 decommission deadline. Acme is explicitly "a Microsoft shop" (§1) already running Power BI for 600 users — this design meets them on infrastructure they already operate and trust, rather than asking them to adopt a second full serving stack.

§2.1's ML pipeline requirement (predictive maintenance, planned) is also cleanly met: the BTS model registry and feature store sit directly over the same Delta tables we're already landing, no separate data movement required.

2. Delivery risk case

This is the smallest build of the three. We are not standing up cross-region active-active infrastructure (Candidate 1) or a warm DR promotion runbook (Candidate 2) — we own one region (West Europe), one ingest path, one lakehouse. The serving tier is Microsoft's to operate, sized, and SLA'd on capacity Acme already owns. Fewer moving parts under BTS control means fewer places for a 14-day-response, 16-week-Teradata-migration timeline to slip. Our 250K events/sec single-region benchmark (per Technical Fit) maps directly onto this design's single-region ingest architecture — unlike a multi-region candidate, we are not asking engineering to validate throughput in a topology we've never tested.

3. Cost case

TCO shape here is materially better than the alternatives, and that matters directly against §3.3's ≥35% mandatory discount and §3.1's 5-year fixed-price-no-escalator term. Every dollar of BTS infrastructure we don't build is a dollar we don't need to discount 35% off and hold flat for five years. We are not carrying the $80–120K/yr active-active add-on cost (Candidate 1), nor the doubled steady-state compute/Event Hubs spend that funds it. Our cost base is essentially: EU ingest tier, EU lakehouse storage, and open-shortcut integration work — a single-region infrastructure bill. That gives Pricing the most room to hit 35% off list and still hold margin across the full 5-year horizon, which is the single hardest commercial constraint in this RFP.

4. Known weakness, addressed head-on

The obvious objection: we're handing the customer-facing layer to Microsoft, who is also bidding this RFP directly (§6). Two responses. First, Acme is already 100% dependent on Microsoft for Power BI today — this design doesn't create that dependency, it inherits a dependency that already exists and that Acme chose. We are not introducing new vendor risk; we're architecting to the estate Acme told us they run (§1: "we are a Microsoft shop"). Second, on renewal exposure: yes, Acme could in theory keep Fabric and replace only our ingest/lakehouse tier — but that cuts both ways. The lakehouse, the 30+ ETL connectors, the Teradata migration tooling, and the ML model registry/feature store are where the actual engineering investment and switching cost live, not the query layer. A competitor displacing us would still need to replace the hardest 80% of the platform.

On the SLA point specifically (§4.3, 99.99%, any miss = immediate termination): I'll flag rather than paper over it — an end-to-end SLA here is a chained commitment across BTS and Microsoft's Fabric capacity, and we should not warrant a number we don't fully control without Microsoft's SLA terms on Fabric capacity feeding into ours contractually. That needs Legal and Pricing to structure carefully (e.g., SLA scoped to the ingest/lakehouse tier we operate, with Fabric's own SLA cited separately for the serving tier), but it is a contract-drafting problem, not a reason to reject the architecture — and it's a problem every candidate in this RFP has to solve at some SLA layer, since none of us hits 99.99% on standard tier per Technical Fit.

Round 2

Peer refutation

Attack only — no advocate defends its own candidate. This is what the skeptic scored from.
Refutation Memo — Advocate 1
Attacking Candidate 2 and Candidate 3
vs. Candidate 2 — EU-Primary Zone-Redundant with Warm US East DR

Candidate 2's entire Round 1 case rests on relitigating §4.3 rather than meeting it. Their own paper admits "this design lands at our standard Enterprise tier — 99.95% monthly uptime — not the 99.99% Acme asks for," and their remedy is to ask Legal to negotiate away the very clause the RFP treats as a tripwire: "any SLA miss, any duration, immediate termination plus full refund." That is not a commercial lever, it is asking Acme to waive the one clause they wrote with zero ambiguity. Nothing in the RFP text — quoted by every advocate in this debate, including them — signals Acme is open to softening it; §4.3 reads as drafted specifically to prevent vendors from doing exactly what Candidate 2 proposes. If Acme declines that negotiation (the likely case for a clause this deliberately absolute), Candidate 2 has no fallback architecture in their paper — they staked the entire SLA gap on a legal ask they have no evidence Acme will grant.

Their "4.3 hours vs 52 minutes" framing also undercuts their own audit story: they tout single-region residency as easier to prove under §4.2's unannounced audits, but a design that structurally cannot clear §4.3 doesn't get to an audit conversation — it gets terminated on the first qualifying outage, audit rights moot. And their cost case leans on "no steady-state cross-region egress" and "no Event Hubs Dedicated capacity duplicated," but that saving is the exact same $80–120K/yr figure they concede is what closes their own SLA gap "cheaper" — they're pricing the uplift as optional while simultaneously admitting it may not be enough to hit 99.99% at all, since their own uplift proposal (tighter health probes, faster failover tuning) is bounded by remaining single-region, which cannot structurally clear four-nines against a regional outage.

vs. Candidate 3 — Fabric-Fronted Hybrid

Candidate 3's own weakness section concedes the SLA problem is worse for them than for anyone else in this debate, not equivalent:

"an end-to-end SLA here is a chained commitment across BTS and Microsoft's Fabric capacity, and we should not warrant a number we don't fully control without Microsoft's SLA terms on Fabric capacity feeding into ours contractually."

That's not a drafting nuance — it means Candidate 3 cannot even propose a §4.3-compliant number today because they don't control half the stack the SLA has to cover. Their suggested fix, "scope the SLA to the ingest/lakehouse tier we operate, with Fabric's own SLA cited separately," directly collides with §4.3's language, which Candidate 2 also quotes: any SLA failure "of any duration" triggers termination — Acme's clause doesn't contemplate a bifurcated SLA with two vendors pointing fingers at each other over which tier missed. A chained, two-vendor SLA is a harder commitment to hold at 99.99%, not an easier one, since uptime under a chain is the product of both parties' availability, not the max.

Second, their §6 admission that "Microsoft is also bidding this RFP directly" is a self-inflicted wound they try to spin as symmetry ("we're not introducing new vendor risk, we're inheriting it") — but architecting our own competitive proposal to be functionally dependent on the party we're competing against for the same deal is a strategic liability no amount of "switching cost lives in the lakehouse" reasoning erases: Microsoft has every incentive, mid-contract, to make their own direct Fabric-native pitch look better than a BTS layer sitting on top of it.

Third, their delivery-risk case claims the smallest build ("we own one region… fewer moving parts under BTS control") while simultaneously outsourcing the RFP's single non-negotiable requirement (§2.3 Power BI for 600 users) to a third party's capacity planning and roadmap — that's not reduced delivery risk, it's delivery risk relocated to a vendor we don't control and can't commit on Acme's behalf.

Refutation Memo — Advocate 2
Attacking Candidate 1 and Candidate 3
vs. Candidate 1 — Dual-Region Active-Active

Their own delivery risk section admits the fatal gap: "we have not validated multi-region throughput at the 80K events/sec peak this design depends on to make its uptime and headroom claims credible," and they recommend an "engineering validation spike" be scoped into the proposal's early milestones — meaning they are asking Acme to award a contract before we know whether the architecture actually works at the scale it's proposing. That is not a delivery risk footnote, it is a proposal that cannot state its own throughput number with confidence on day one, against a 14-day response window and a 2026-06-30 award target.

Worse, their cost section concedes the doubled steady-state compute and Event Hubs spend is real and must be "priced correctly" and "modeled explicitly" against the 5-year fixed-price, no-escalator term in §3.1 — but they never show that model, they just assert margin can absorb it. And their residency pitch for §4.2 audits — "an auditor can point at a table and get a single, provable answer" — still requires proving, across every audit cycle for five years, that "replication explicitly disabled at the table level" has never failed open on the non-EU side of a bidirectional sync. That's a standing control to defend indefinitely, not a one-time architectural fact.

vs. Candidate 3 — Fabric-Fronted Hybrid

Their own Round 1 paper flags, in their words, that they should "not warrant a number we don't fully control without Microsoft's SLA terms on Fabric capacity feeding into ours contractually" — under §4.3's language, any SLA miss of any duration triggers immediate termination and full refund. They are proposing to hand the customer-facing serving tier — the layer 600 analysts actually touch every day — to a third party's SLA that BTS doesn't own, control, or have visibility into for cure/remediation, and then ask Legal to carve the SLA into two scoped pieces post-hoc. That's not a contract-drafting problem they can wave off as "every candidate has to solve this somehow" — it's a unique structural exposure only their design creates, since Candidate 1 and this candidate both keep the full stack under BTS control.

And their own §6 admission is worse than they present it: Microsoft is bidding this RFP directly, and Candidate 3's architecture makes BTS's entire serving layer a rent-paid dependency on the very competitor sitting across the table from Acme in the same procurement. Their rebuttal — "Acme already depends on Microsoft for Power BI" — doesn't address that; today Acme controls that dependency directly, whereas this design inserts BTS as a reseller-layer intermediary on top of a competitor's platform, with no contractual leverage of our own if Microsoft decides to make life difficult for a Fabric-hybrid partner during a live competitive RFP cycle.

Refutation Memo — Advocate 3
Attacking Candidate 1 and Candidate 2
vs. Candidate 1 — Dual-Region Active-Active

Candidate 1's own delivery risk section admits the disqualifying fact: "our 250K events/sec ingest benchmark is single-region only. We have not validated multi-region throughput at the 80K events/sec peak this design depends on." That is not a minor caveat — it is the entire uptime and headroom argument in Section 1 resting on an unvalidated number, by their own admission, and they recommend an "engineering validation spike" be scoped in before pricing goes to Acme. Under a 14-day RFP response window and 2026-06-30 award target, there is no time to run that spike before commitment; they are asking Deal Desk to quote a 99.99% SLA — the exact clause whose breach triggers immediate termination and full refund under §4.3 — on top of a throughput claim their own advocate says isn't proven at the topology they're proposing.

Their cost section is equally self-undermining: they concede this "roughly doubles steady-state compute and Event Hubs Dedicated spend" and that this "compresses margin hard" against the §3.3 ≥35% floor and §3.1's five-year no-escalator term, then wave it off as "a pricing decision for Deal Desk, not an architecture flaw." That's a distinction without a difference — if the architecture structurally requires margin compression Pricing can't absorb across five fixed years, that's a scope failure dressed up as a commercial exercise.

Their audit answer is also weaker than they present it: "replication explicitly disabled at the table level" for EU residency is a control that has to be verified as never having failed open, every one of the four unannounced audits a year (§4.2) — a negative proof, not the one-sentence "no copy exists" answer a single-region design gives an auditor.

vs. Candidate 2 — EU-Primary Warm DR

Candidate 2 spends its entire Section 4 building an elaborate case for negotiating away the exact clause the RFP flags as most severe. They call it "closeable" and cite it as "roughly 4.3 hours vs 52 minutes of downtime per month" — but that framing quietly concedes their standard tier misses the 99.99% target in §4.3 by design, and §4.3's language is not ambiguous: "any duration shall entitle Acme to terminate the contract immediately, with full refund of fees paid in the affected month." Their proposed fix — "a scoped SLA credit/cure structure negotiated into §4.3 rather than accepted as literal zero-tolerance" — asks Legal to persuade Acme to soften the single contractual term the customer wrote in the most unequivocal language in the entire RFP, on a deal where Acme already holds termination leverage. That is a bet on a negotiation outcome, not a technical answer, and it is being proposed as a substitute for meeting the requirement rather than a fallback.

Their DR posture is also softer than their audit argument implies: a "warm" DR region with "async replication and a documented runbook" means a regional failure event is a promotion, not an instant failover — during that promotion window, they are exposed to the exact SLA clock their own Section 4 admits they can't currently clear even in steady state. And their delivery risk pitch — "the fastest of the three candidates to stand up" — is the same one-active-region, one-ingest-path profile as the hybrid approach, minus the advantage of running the serving tier on infrastructure Acme already owns and operates today; they're taking on the full BTS-owned serving stack build without the residency-simplicity payoff they claim, since their DR region still holds a "replicated hot/recent subset" of data that has to be reasoned about under §2.3's EU-residency clause the same way any cross-region copy does.

Step 4 — Commercial scoring (arch_commercial)

Scale 1–10 per dimension, 10 = most favorable to BTS commercially. Weighted total = TCO×0.20 + Delivery Risk×0.40 + Margin Exposure×0.40. The skeptic champions none of the three and introduces no new architectural claims.

Rubric — TCO: 5-year infrastructure + operations cost, relative. Delivery risk: likelihood of missing the RFP's implementation milestones given team familiarity, integration surface, and unknowns surfaced in refutation. Margin exposure: cost-overrun risk carried if quoted inside a 5-year fixed price.

Scoring rationale — Candidate 1 2.0 / 10 · bottom of the field on all three axes

On TCO, even its own advocate concedes it "roughly doubles steady-state compute and Event Hubs Dedicated spend" plus egress/replication — this is the most expensive build by a wide margin, with no offsetting scope reduction anywhere else.

On delivery risk, the advocate's own Round 1 paper admits the disqualifying fact that both refutation memos seize on: "our 250K events/sec ingest benchmark is single-region only. We have not validated multi-region throughput at the 80K events/sec peak this design depends on" — and the proposed fix is an "engineering validation spike" scoped into early milestones, i.e. asking Acme to award before we know the architecture works at the scale its own uptime case depends on, against a 14-day response window and a 2026-06-30 award target. That is a proposal with an open technical question at its load-bearing center.

On margin exposure, the advocate calls the doubled spend "a pricing decision for Deal Desk, not an architecture flaw" but never produces the model — the rebuttal correctly calls this "a distinction without a difference." Layered on top: the EU/non-EU replication-disabled control has to be proven never to have failed open at every one of four unannounced audits a year, for five years — a standing negative-proof burden, not a one-time fact, adding ongoing compliance cost risk on top of the doubled infrastructure spend.

Scoring rationale — Candidate 2 5.8 / 10 · clear TCO winner, dragged by the SLA gap

Clear winner on TCO — single active compute/storage plane, no duplicated Event Hubs Dedicated capacity, no steady-state cross-region egress on the full EU dataset, DR scaled down rather than warm-active — which the advocate correctly ties to giving Pricing "the most room to clear the §3.3 floor of ≥35% off list while preserving margin." It also uses the one benchmark that actually matches its topology (250K events/sec single-region, tested, against an 80K events/sec single-region target), making it the fastest and least novel build of the three — standard zone-redundant patterns, not active-active multi-write metadata.

But delivery risk is dragged down hard by a gap neither refutation lets stand: the design structurally cannot meet the 99.99% SLA in §4.3, and the advocate's own remedy is to have Legal negotiate away "the exact clause the RFP flags as most severe" — a clause the rebuttal notes reads as "drafted specifically to prevent vendors from doing exactly what Candidate 2 proposes," with "no fallback architecture" if Acme declines.

On margin exposure this cuts both ways: steady-state economics are the best of the three, but §4.3's termination-plus-full-refund trigger is a binary, catastrophic tail risk sitting directly on top of that favorable cost base, and the DR promotion window itself (manual runbook, not instant failover) is exposed to the same SLA clock the design admits it can't clear even in steady state.

Scoring rationale — Candidate 3 4.2 / 10 · TCO tie, but structurally worse SLA exposure

Ties Candidate 2 on TCO — smallest BTS infrastructure footprint of the three ("EU ingest tier, EU lakehouse storage, and open-shortcut integration work — a single-region infrastructure bill"), no active-active add-on, no doubled compute — giving Pricing similar room against the 35% discount floor and five-year fixed price.

But delivery risk is materially worse than its small build size suggests, per the refutations: the smallest-BTS-footprint claim is undercut by outsourcing the RFP's single non-negotiable requirement (§2.3 Power BI for 600 users) to "a vendor we don't control and can't commit on Acme's behalf," and the design depends on "cross-tenant OneLake shortcut behaviour and Fabric capacity sizing that we have neither benchmarked nor priced" — an unvalidated dependency layered on top of relying on Microsoft, who is bidding this same RFP directly (§6).

Margin exposure inherits the worst version of Candidate 2's SLA problem: the advocate concedes "we should not warrant a number we don't fully control without Microsoft's SLA terms," and the rebuttal correctly notes a two-vendor chained SLA is harder to hit 99.99% on than a single-vendor gap ("the product of both parties' availability, not the max"), while §4.5 subprocessor consent and split §4.2 audit governance across two organizations add contractual exposure the other two candidates don't carry. Favorable steady-state cost is offset by a termination-trigger risk that is structurally worse than Candidate 2's, not better.

Step 5 — Judgment

Judge: deal-desk-orchestrator, reading all three position papers, all refutations and the commercial scoring.

★ Winner

Candidate 2 — EU-primary zone-redundant lakehouse with warm US East DR

Topology

One active region, West Europe, across three AZs: zone-redundant Event Hubs Dedicated and AKS-hosted ingest, ZRS ADLS Gen2 holding the full ~280TB Delta/Iceberg corpus, zone-redundant metadata and catalog services. East US 2 runs a warm standby — provisioned but scaled down, receiving async replication of non-EU-classified tables only (RPO ~15 min), promoted by runbook on regional failure. EU-classified data never leaves West Europe, making residency trivially provable: the DR region simply has no copy. US East doubles as a read-only serving footprint so Austin analysts get local Power BI DirectQuery against a replicated hot/recent subset. Ingest, batch ETL and the Teradata cutover all terminate in the single EU primary — exactly one authoritative write path.

Optimised for

§2.2 scale and §2.1 workloads at the lowest defensible cost, serving the RFP's 20% TCO and 15% implementation-timeline-and-risk criteria; §2.3 EU residency in the cleanest possible form (one-copy, one-region); §7 implementation timeline — fastest of the three to stand up and the one our engineering has actually benchmarked, since the 250K events/sec single-region test maps directly onto it.

Carried weakness — must be handled commercially

It structurally cannot reach 99.99%. Zone-redundant single-region lands at our standard 99.95% Enterprise tier, and under §4.3 any SLA miss of any duration triggers immediate termination plus full refund of that month's fees. It also only partially satisfies §2.3's "multi-region deployment" — a warm passive DR region is arguably not what Acme means — and the DR promotion runbook introduces a manual RTO that a zero-tolerance SLA clause will not forgive. Legal and Pricing must resolve §4.3 (cure period / scoped termination trigger) before this goes out.

Why each loser lost

Candidate 1 — Dual-region active-active lakehouse

2.0 / 10 Lost on commercial score TCO 2 · Delivery 2 · Margin 2

Two refutation memos independently seized on the same self-admitted, load-bearing gap: "our 250K events/sec ingest benchmark is single-region only. We have not validated multi-region throughput at the 80K events/sec peak this design depends on." Its remedy — an engineering validation spike scoped into early milestones — asks Acme to award a contract before we know the architecture works at the scale its entire 99.99% uptime case rests on, against a 14-day response window and a 2026-06-30 award target.

On margin, the advocate dismissed roughly doubled steady-state compute and Event Hubs Dedicated spend as "a pricing decision for Deal Desk, not an architecture flaw" and never produced the model; the refutation correctly called this "a distinction without a difference" — an architecture that structurally requires margin compression Pricing cannot absorb across five fixed, no-escalator years (§3.1) under a ≥35% discount floor (§3.3) is a scope failure, not a pricing exercise.

Its §4.2 audit story is also weaker than claimed: "replication explicitly disabled at the table level" is a standing negative-proof burden to defend at four unannounced audits a year for five years, not a one-time architectural fact.

Candidate 3 — Fabric-fronted hybrid

4.2 / 10 Lost on delivery risk + margin TCO 9 · Delivery 3 · Margin 3

Delivery risk 3 and margin exposure 3 wiped out its TCO tie (9) with the winner. The decisive refutation point: it "cannot even propose a §4.3-compliant number today because they don't control half the stack the SLA has to cover" — the advocate itself conceded "we should not warrant a number we don't fully control without Microsoft's SLA terms on Fabric capacity feeding into ours contractually."

Its proposed fix — bifurcating the SLA between BTS ingest/lakehouse and Fabric serving — collides head-on with §4.3's "any duration" termination language, which does not contemplate two vendors pointing at each other. A chained SLA is arithmetically harder, not easier: "the product of both parties' availability, not the max" — making its termination-trigger exposure structurally worse than Candidate 2's, not equivalent.

Compounding this: it outsources the RFP's single explicitly non-negotiable requirement (§2.3 Power BI for 600 users) to Microsoft, a named competing bidder under §6, so the smallest-build delivery-risk claim is delivery risk merely relocated to a vendor we don't control; and it depends on cross-tenant OneLake shortcut behaviour and Fabric capacity sizing we have neither benchmarked nor priced, while §4.5 subprocessor consent and split §4.2 audit governance add contractual exposure the other two candidates do not carry.
